title: What does @Transactional(readOnly=true) optimize, how does it relate to dirty checking, and why is Open Session In View an anti-pattern?
topicTitle: Performance — Large IN, Dirty Checking, OSIV

s1_definition.profdef: `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` hints that a transaction performs no writes, allowing Hibernate to skip dirty-checking (setting FlushMode to MANUAL/NEVER) and letting the driver/database route to read replicas and apply read-only optimizations. Open Session In View (OSIV) keeps the persistence context open for the entire HTTP request so lazy associations can be loaded in the view layer; it is an anti-pattern because it holds database connections longer, hides N+1 problems, and blurs transaction boundaries.
s1_definition.analogy: readOnly=true is like telling the bank clerk "I'm only here to look, not to change anything." The clerk then skips the slow double-checking of whether anything was edited (dirty checking) and can send you to a faster "viewing-only" counter (a read replica). OSIV is like leaving the vault door open for your entire visit so you can keep fetching more files whenever you remember them — convenient, but it ties up the vault and the clerk far too long, and you never notice you are making a hundred trips instead of one.
s1_definition.oneliner: readOnly=true skips dirty checking and enables replica reads; OSIV keeps the session open too long and hides N+1 — avoid it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` hints that a transaction performs no writes, allowing Hibernate to skip dirty-checking (setting FlushMode to MANUAL/NEVER) and letting the driver/database route to read replicas and apply read-only optimizations. Open Session In View (OSIV) keeps the persistence context open for the entire HTTP request so lazy associations can be loaded in the view layer; it is an anti-pattern because it holds database connections longer, hides N+1 problems, and blurs transaction boundaries.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** readOnly=true is like telling the bank clerk "I'm only here to look, not to change anything." The clerk then skips the slow double-checking of whether anything was edited (dirty checking) and can send you to a faster "viewing-only" counter (a read replica). OSIV is like leaving the vault door open for your entire visit so you can keep fetching more files whenever you remember them — convenient, but it ties up the vault and the clerk far too long, and you never notice you are making a hundred trips instead of one.

**One line to remember:** readOnly=true skips dirty checking and enables replica reads; OSIV keeps the session open too long and hides N+1 — avoid it.

sections.s2_technical:
Dirty checking is how Hibernate detects changes: it snapshots each managed entity on load and, at flush, compares current state to the snapshot to generate UPDATEs. For a pure read this comparison is wasted work. `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` sets the Hibernate FlushMode to MANUAL so no automatic flush/dirty-check happens, reducing CPU and avoiding accidental writes. It also sets the JDBC connection read-only, which some databases and poolers use to route to read replicas and relax locking.

For example, a balance-enquiry service method annotated `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` loads Rajesh's account, reads the balance, and returns — Hibernate does not snapshot-compare or attempt any UPDATE. If buggy code sets a field, nothing is persisted because there is no flush.

OSIV (spring.jpa.open-in-view, default true in Spring Boot) binds the Hibernate Session to the request thread for the whole request, including view rendering. The upside is lazy associations load in the controller or template without a LazyInitializationException. The downsides are serious: the database connection is held from controller through view rendering, reducing pool availability under load; lazy loads in the view trigger invisible queries, masking N+1 problems that explode query counts; and the transaction boundary no longer cleanly maps to the service method, so what should be read-only can issue queries outside any explicit transaction.

The recommended pattern is to disable OSIV (`spring.jpa.open-in-view=false`) and fetch everything you need inside the service transaction using fetch joins or DTO projections, returning fully initialized objects or DTOs to the controller. This makes the query count explicit, releases connections promptly, and keeps transaction boundaries clear.

Senior nuances: readOnly=true does not make the database truly read-only for all engines, but it is a strong optimization and safety hint; combine it with projections for best read performance. Turning OSIV off forces you to design fetch strategies deliberately, which is a feature, not a burden.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Thousands of customers check their balance every minute. Each enquiry is a pure read, yet dirty checking still snapshots and compares. This wastes CPU. This is exactly what readOnly=true optimizes away.

Problem 2 — Balance enquiries should hit a read replica to spare the primary database. readOnly=true sets the connection read-only so routing can send it to a replica.

Problem 3 — A statement view lazily loads each transaction's account inside the template, firing hundreds of hidden queries. This N+1 is masked by OSIV. The fix is to disable OSIV and fetch-join in the service.

We will build a BalanceService (readOnly) and a StatementService that fetch-joins instead of relying on OSIV.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run (OSIV disabled in config)
java -jar target/readonly-txn-service-1.0.0.jar

# Balance enquiry (read-only optimized)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001/balance

# Statement (fetch-joined, no N+1)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001/statement
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: balance enquiry for SAV2001; statement for SAV2001 with 3 transactions.

Step 1 — balanceOf runs in a readOnly transaction. Hibernate sets FlushMode to MANUAL and the JDBC connection to read-only. It loads SAV2001 and returns the balance.

Step 2 — At the end of balanceOf, there is no flush and no dirty-check snapshot comparison, so even if code accidentally mutated a field, nothing would be written. CPU is saved and the connection could have been routed to a replica.

Step 3 — statement runs findWithTxns, which executes a single left-join-fetch query loading the account and all its transactions together. The txns collection is fully initialized before the transaction ends.

Step 4 — Because OSIV is disabled, the session closes when the service method returns. The controller receives a fully initialized list, so rendering the view triggers zero extra queries — the N+1 that OSIV would have hidden simply cannot occur.

```
INFO  Balance enquiry SAV2001 = 1000000      (readOnly, no flush)
Hibernate: select a.* from accounts a where id=?
Hibernate: select a.*, t.* from accounts a left join txns t on ... where a.id=?
INFO  Statement SAV2001 loaded 3 txns in ONE query
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Balance enquiry SAV2001
    │
    ▼
  BalanceService (@Transactional readOnly=true)
    │ FlushMode=MANUAL, connection read-only
    │ load account, read balance
    ▼ no flush, no dirty check → replica-routable
  Response: balance=1,000,000

  Statement SAV2001 (OSIV disabled)
    │
    ▼
  StatementService (@Transactional readOnly)
    │ findWithTxns → LEFT JOIN FETCH (ONE query)
    │ txns initialized inside txn
    ▼ session closes at method end
  Controller/view → ZERO extra queries (no N+1)

  (With OSIV: view would lazy-load each txn.account → N+1 hidden)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Read-Only Transactions + OSIV Off ═══

  ┌────────┐ REST ┌─────────────┐ REST ┌────────────────────┐
  │ NetBank│─────→│ API Gateway │─────→│ Read Service ×6     │
  │ (reads)│      │ cache       │      │ readOnly=true       │
  └────────┘      └─────────────┘      └─────────┬──────────┘
                   readOnly routed to replica     │ JDBC
                                 ┌─────────────────┴───────────┐
                                 ▼ writes                      ▼ reads
                       ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐
                       │ PostgreSQL Primary│  WAL →  │ Read Replica ×2   │
                       └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘
  OSIV disabled → connections released at service end → higher pool throughput.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — readOnly + dirty checking + OSIV ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Unit of Work: persistence context = txn boundary    │
  │ Fetch-join strategy replaces OSIV lazy loading      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: BalanceService reads only                        │
  │ D: depends on repository abstraction                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        BalanceService         │
  │  @Transactional(readOnly=true)│ FlushMode=MANUAL
  │  + balanceOf(id): BigDecimal  │ no dirty check
  └───────────────────────────────┘
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       StatementService        │
  │  + statement(id): List<Txn>   │ fetch-join (no OSIV)
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Trade-off: OSIV on vs off ──
  OSIV on  → lazy loads in view (hidden N+1, long connection hold)
  OSIV off → must fetch-join in service (explicit queries, fast release)

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. balanceOf(SAV2001) → findById → read balance (no flush)
  2. statement(SAV2001) → findWithTxns (1 join query)
  3. session closes → view renders with ZERO extra queries
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The readOnly flag on Transactional is both a performance optimization and a safety guard. When I mark a method read-only, Hibernate sets the flush mode to manual, which means it skips dirty checking entirely. Normally Hibernate snapshots every loaded entity and, at flush time, compares the current state to the snapshot to generate updates; for a pure read that comparison is wasted CPU, and skipping it is a real saving under heavy read load. It also sets the JDBC connection to read-only, which many databases and connection poolers use to route the query to a read replica and relax locking. As a bonus, if buggy code accidentally mutates a loaded entity, nothing is persisted because there is no flush.

Open Session In View is the anti-pattern I actively disable. With OSIV on, Spring binds the Hibernate session to the whole HTTP request, including view rendering, so lazy associations can be loaded in the controller or template without a lazy-initialization exception. That convenience hides three real problems: the database connection is held from the controller all the way through view rendering, which starves the pool under load; lazy loads in the view fire invisible queries that mask N+1 problems; and the transaction boundary no longer maps cleanly to the service method.

In our National Bank of India system, balance enquiries are pure reads happening thousands of times a minute, so I annotate them read-only to skip dirty checking and let them route to a read replica. For the statement view I disable OSIV and instead fetch everything I need inside the service transaction using a left-join-fetch, so the controller receives a fully initialized list and rendering the page triggers zero extra queries. The N+1 that OSIV would have quietly hidden simply cannot happen.

The senior position I take is that turning OSIV off is a feature, not a burden, because it forces me to design fetch strategies deliberately with fetch joins or DTO projections and makes the query count explicit and reviewable. Combined with read-only transactions and projections, this gives fast, predictable reads with connections released promptly, which is exactly what a high-traffic banking read path needs.

---

keyPoints: @Transactional(readOnly=true): no dirty checking, JPA hint to DB
Dirty checking cost: proportional to number of managed entities
Without OSIV: use JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph for lazy collections
